South Facade Billboard: Christina Leslie.name: South Facade Billboard: Christina Leslie
South Facade Billboard: Christina Leslie.description: The South Facade Billboard is an ongoing series of photographic works that resonate with the context within which they are presented on the lake-facing exterior wall of the gallery. For this edition, The Power Plant has partnered with ERA Architects to showcase the work of artist Christina Leslie in a presentation that aligns with the goals of Art=Waterfront, an ERA-led initiative that identifies the waterfront as a vital space to foster and celebrate the city’s artistic and cultural landscape. Part of Leslie’s photographic series Pinhole Parishes (2023-25), the selected image, _Pinhole 11_, explores memory, place, and intergenerational connection through the lens of her Jamaican heritage. Drawing inspiration from stories and memories shared by relatives, Leslie's images create a dialogue between past and present, reconstructing familial and cultural histories shaped by migration, geography, and fragmented archives. At once a personal act of remembrance and a broader act of reclamation, the series maps stories across all fourteen civil territorial divisions in Jamaica known as parishes. **About the Artist** **Christina Leslie** (b. 1983) is a Pickering-based photographic artist. She holds a BFA from OCAD University (2006) and an MFA from the Savannah College of Art and Design (2022). Leslie has exhibited at institutions including GAMU in Prague, Oakland University in Michigan, the Royal Ontario Museum, BAND Gallery, Canada’s Pier 21, the Art Gallery of Windsor, Prefix Photo, the McMaster Museum of Art, MOCA Toronto, and many others. Recent exhibitions include Likkle Acts at the Robert McLaughlin Gallery (2024–2025) and Pinhole Portraits and Places at Stephen Bulger Gallery (2025). She also served as Interim Assistant Curator at the McMaster Museum of Art, curating THE GREAT UNSEEN(2025). Her photographs are held in private, corporate, and institutional collections, and she is represented by Stephen Bulger Gallery in Toronto.

Colourful Parachutes: Imagining Alternat.name: Colourful Parachutes: Imagining Alternative Futures Through the Power of Play
Colourful Parachutes: Imagining Alternat.description: _Colourful Parachutes: Imagining Alternative Futures Through the Power of Play_ brings together leading artists from Canada and abroad to examine the politics of the exhibition space through the radical power of play. Imagining children as the exhibition’s primary audience, it puts into question how we make, present, and experience contemporary art—often with unexpected and uniquely engaging results. Influenced by exhibitions like Palle Nielsen’s _The Model_ (1968), which turned Stockholm’s Moderna Museet into a giant adventure playground, _Colourful Parachutes_ views the gallery as a microcosm of society. If we allow children to reinvent it, what new worlds can we co-create? A key theme underlying _Colourful Parachutes_ is the relationship young people have to the future. Many of the works in the exhibition touch on the vital importance of fostering a relationship to the natural world during childhood, the increasing sense of eco-anxiety carried by young people, and how to advocate for child-led environmental activism. The title is borrowed from Ailton Krenak’s book _Ideas to Postpone the End of the World_ (2019), in which the Brazilian Indigenous philosopher and environmental activist suggests using creativity and dreaming to create colourful parachutes that might slow our fall. Krenak asks: “What sort of world are you boxing and wrapping for future generations? You keep talking about another world, but have you asked the generations of tomorrow if the world you’re building is the world they want?” Including several participatory, interactive works, _Colourful Parachutes_ transforms the gallery into a space where things can be made, moved, played with, tried out, tested, and touched. By disrupting the formal conventions that we are accustomed to in the gallery, it encourages people of all ages to become active participants in the shaping of their environment by giving them the power to envision a different world for us all.

Fogo-The Power Plant.name: Fogo
Fogo-The Power Plant.description: Over the course of four summers spent on Newfoundland’s Fogo Island, at Canada’s easternmost reaches, Sharon Lockhart developed a series of photographs and a film building upon core themes that have continued to define her career: an exploration of place, a durational approach to attention, and a long-term commitment to those who appear before her lens. This exhibition features her series of photographs, collectively entitled _Fogo Island Portrait Studio_, that pictures the island’s young residents. Working with these same protagonists, Lockhart also created _WINDWARD_—a film installation that brings to life the island’s striking geological formations, unique climate, and austere beauty. _WINDWARD_, Lockhart’s filmic exploration of Fogo’s present, sees time as it shifts and envelops, surging and calming in pace with the ever-present winds that shape life on the island. Finding precedent in Colin Low’s 1967 documentary _The Children of Fogo Island_—a symbol of the island’s past, witnessing youth as they interacted within their communities—Lockhart carefully observes the island’s geography, directing its youth in play amid fields of tall grass, volcanic rocks, and crashing waves. The sea, sky, light, and weather become essential in shaping its set of 12 compositions. Vastness takes hold as figures are made minute, appearing at distance in evocations of those that populate landscape painting of centuries past. Filmed on the island’s northern face—its windward end—the work takes cues from an unseen force: persistent gusts that descend from the Arctic, arriving on land as undeniable presences. In scenes choreographed from observation, the children of _WINDWARD_ move in and out of sight, exploring Lockhart’s tableaux in their entireties. An inherited attunement to the environment, the ability to read and heed it, comes to the fore across Lockhart’s photography and film, poetically encapsulating perseverance in the face of a modern world. _Fogo Island Portrait Studio_, the result of an open invitation to the artist’s studio, housed in a refashioned fishing shed, sees the island’s children in seven formal encounters with a still camera. Here, Lockhart presents daylit portraits; their singular subjects framed nonhierarchically to occupy equal space within each image. Posed with striking directness, the children possess a focus that counters the speed and omnipresence of mobile-phone image making. Against black backgrounds, they assert a decided agency, positioning themselves as active participants in shaping their futures. This exhibition sees Lockhart return to The Power Plant for a second presentation, following her 2010 solo exhibition _Podwórka_, which took as its subject matter children playing in abandoned urban areas in Łódź, Poland.

Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echo.name: Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes: Your Ancestors Are Whales, and Earth Remembers Everything
Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echo.description: _Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes: Your Ancestors Are Whales, and Earth Remembers Everything_ is an exhibition by Vancouver-born, UK-based artist Zadie Xa, made together with her long-term collaborator, artist Benito Mayor Vallejo. The exhibition includes new paintings alongside works from the 2024 exhibition _Rough Hands Weave a Knife_ and _Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes: Your Ancestors Are Whales, and Earth Remembers Everything_, an immersive installation by Xa and Mayor Vallejo presented at the Sharjah Biennial 16 in 2025, which won the artist a nomination for the prestigious Turner Prize that same year. These works continue Xa’s ongoing exploration of diasporic identity, hybrid spaces, Korean mythology and folklore, the power of storytelling, and the deep interconnections that bind us to non-human worlds. Expansive and multilayered, the exhibition combines a range of media—including a sound installation, a hand-painted mural of saturated twilight colours, and delicate bronze sculptures of hybrid figures dancing between human and animal worlds, co-authored by both artists—with intimate and large-scale paintings by Xa that often incorporate textile panels evoking traditional Korean patchwork quilting. Across this varied landscape, several narratives recur. One is a fascination with matriarchal subjects. Many of Xa’s paintings show female figures in spiritual or mystical scenes. They conjure visions of forested or undersea landscapes, the practice of Salpuri (a traditional Korean spirit-cleansing dance rooted in shamanic rituals), or commune with fantastical creatures and messengers from other worlds. A frequent motif in Xa’s work that also has a presence here is the whale, and in particular a certain species of orca that passes ancestral knowledge down to younger generations through its matrilineal elders. Animals are just as likely to take centre stage in _Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes: Your Ancestors Are Whales, and Earth Remembers Everything_ as their human counterparts. These include treasured domestic pets, but also creatures subsisting on the margins of human society, such as the seagull and the fox. A cultural shapeshifter, foxes hold deep significance in Korean culture but are also ubiquitous in the urban landscapes of Xa’s London home. As in a parable or fairy tale, these creatures can be understood as instructional figures or interlocutors. They take us between worlds and offer us much-needed guidance at this critical moment of ecological frailty. The ocean is another guiding theme within the exhibition. Connecting South Korea, Canada’s West Coast and the United Kingdom, the deep sea is evoked here through depictions of marine creatures, through the glint of mother of pearl, and through recurring references to seashells. The seashell motif is echoed in a number of works co-authored by Xa and Mayor Vallejo, including a spoken narrative heard through four suspended shells, and a mobile made of over six hundred brass bells traditionally used in Korean shamanic rituals, hung from the gallery’s ceiling in the spiral shape of a conch.

Owner of a Lonely Heart-The Power Plant.name: Owner of a Lonely Heart
Owner of a Lonely Heart-The Power Plant.description: The Power Plant and The Vega Foundation present _Owner of a Lonely Heart_, a program of recent moving image works by contemporary artists Haig Aivazian, Stephanie Comilang, Alia Farid, Hope Pearl Strickland, and Yuyan Wang. On view in The Power Plant’s North Gallery, the 80-minute program cycles on a loop, moving from documentary, narrative, and archival approaches to filmmaking toward increasingly associative, musical, and rhythmic forms. The artists’ works trace the movement of raw materials drawn from the earth, transformed into products, and transported by waterways–be they petroleum, pearls, or plastic plants. Each work portrays a dense web of relations linking labour, ecosystems, and global economies. By tracing the transformation of raw matter, the works reveal how people are bound by circumscribed geographies and unevenly shaped by global networks of extraction and circulation. Together, the artists consider how geopolitical histories shape social and collective identity, and how individuals locate themselves within an overwhelming present. When the prosperity and stability experienced in one place is enabled by the exploitation and scarcity imposed elsewhere, what responsibility does vision bring?

Smokestack Commission Program: Sami Tsan.name: Smokestack Commission Program: Sami Tsang
Smokestack Commission Program: Sami Tsan.description: _What We Carry Forward_ by Toronto-based artist Sami Tsang is the inaugural work in The Power Plant’s Smokestack Commission Program. Tsang is a Chinese-Canadian artist working primarily as a ceramicist. Her work stems from her own narratives as well as the stories she gathers around domestic encounters. Working primarily with ceramics, painting, and metal, Tsang channels these stories into her artmaking to reveal shared, raw, emotional experiences. Drawing from her studio practice, which brings together themes of migration, inheritance, and memory through figurative sculpture and mixed media, Tsang creates a site-specific, large-scale ink mural. Inspired by childhood shadow puppetry and populated by tiny porcelain figurines of girls, the work explores the space between vulnerability and protection, play and strength, memory and becoming. Through the imagined world of fantasy, care, and collective movement, Tsang considers the quieter inheritances women carry through their lives and pass between generations. In this symbolic realm, the materials become part of the story itself: the clay holds the body; the silver protects the spirit.

Fleck Clerestory Commission Program: Ell.name: Fleck Clerestory Commission Program: Ella Gonzales
Fleck Clerestory Commission Program: Ell.description: The Power Plant continues its longstanding Fleck Clerestory Commission Program _A Room’s Proportion, above or below_ by Toronto-based artist Ella Gonzales. Gonzales is a Filipina-Canadian artist working between painting and Computer-Aided Design programs, as led by her interest in space making. Inspired by the concept of displacement that immigrant communities experience, she is known for her paintings on piña silk, a fabric made from the leaves of a pineapple plant that is native to the Philippines Working across painting and architecture, at The Power Plant Gonzales has created her largest installation to date with a site-responsive arrangement of painted chiffon and silk curtains. The work continues her consideration of familial architecture by superimposing remembered proportions onto the Clerestory gallery's distinct structural features. The work transforms the space through layers of translucent fabric based on domestic interior proportions recalled from memory. As one remembered space is superimposed onto another, visitors move through overlapping rooms, histories, and perspectives. Responding to the idea of the threshold, we are invited to consider what happens when one condition slips into another, and how traces of what came before remain visible in what follows.

South Facade Billboard: Morgan Sears-Wil.name: South Facade Billboard: Morgan Sears-Williams
South Facade Billboard: Morgan Sears-Wil.description: This season, The Power Plant Contemporary Art Gallery’s South Facade Billboard presents Toronto- and Vancouver-based artist Morgan Sears-Williams’s feeling along the edges, a work developed during her 2023 residency at Gibraltar Point Centre for the Arts on Mnisiing (the Toronto Islands), across the water from where you are now standing. The image, which consists of several 16mm film strips collated into one frame, captures Hanlan’s Point Beach on the northwestern tip of the islands, a place the artist has been visiting for a decade. Witnessing the gradual geological erosion that is currently occurring there, Sears-Williams filmed the beach, holding the camera at hip height to capture the lakefront and intimate details of the shoreline. She then developed the film in instant coffee and buried it in the sand for five days. The beach residue altered the film’s emulsion, producing scratches, abrasions, and other material artifacts. The tactility of this method of developing film is central to Sears-Williams’s practice and informs her interest in what American feminist filmmaker Barbara Hammer describes as the “feeling image”—a cinematic language in which embodiment, emotion, and image are inextricable. It also situates her work within a lineage of women experimental filmmakers, who have countered conventional cinematic narrative structures and emphasized the craft-based aspects of the medium. The artist’s meditation on the geological erosion of Hanlan’s Point Beach also carries social and cultural implications. For nearly a century, the beach has served as an unofficial site of queer refuge and community. It was also where Toronto’s first-ever Pride celebration took place in August 1971. From the 1970s through the late 1990s, it was subject to significant anti-2SLGBTQI+ harassment and police surveillance, even as queer communities continued to advocate for and reclaim the space. Sears-Williams’s work doubly mourns the precarity of these spaces in Toronto, considering how ecological disintegration is mirrored in the disappearance of longstanding public spaces for queer communities
